facts.subject: random
facts.title: Tardigrade
facts.text: Tardigrades are microscopic animals, mostly under half a millimetre long. When dried into a dormant 'tun' state, they can survive extreme cold and heat, vacuum and strong radiation.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Mantis shrimp
facts.text: Mantis shrimp strike with their club-like limbs at about 23 m/s. The blow is so fast it produces vapor bubbles whose collapse adds a second impact. Their eyes also hold 12 to 16 types of photoreceptor.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Pando (tree)
facts.text: Pando is a single male quaking aspen clone in Utah. Its roughly 47,000 trunks share one root system, and the colony is estimated to be thousands of years old and to weigh about 6,000 tonnes.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Antikythera mechanism
facts.text: The Antikythera mechanism is a hand-cranked ancient Greek device from about the 2nd century BC. Found in a shipwreck in 1901, it modelled the motions of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Difference engine
facts.text: Charles Babbage designed the difference engine in the 1820s to tabulate polynomial values using only addition. It was not finished in his lifetime, but the Science Museum later built a working section of his Difference Engine No. 2.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Rosetta Stone
facts.text: The Rosetta Stone carries one 196 BC decree written in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, it became the key that helped Champollion decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs in the 1820s.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Terracotta Army
facts.text: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an found the Terracotta Army in 1974. These buried clay figures, numbering several thousand soldiers, were made to accompany China's first emperor in the afterlife.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Lake Baikal
facts.text: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake on Earth, reaching about 1,642 metres. It holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Mariana Trench
facts.text: The Mariana Trench lies in the western Pacific, east of the Mariana Islands. Its deepest known point, Challenger Deep, is nearly 11,000 metres below sea level.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Voyager Golden Record
facts.text: Each Voyager probe launched in 1977 carries a gold-plated copper disk. It holds greetings, music, natural sounds and 116 images meant to portray life and culture on Earth to any finder.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Great Red Spot
facts.text: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm, the largest anticyclone in the Solar System. It is about 1.3 times as wide as Earth, and it has been slowly shrinking for over a century.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Seven Bridges of Königsberg
facts.text: In 1736 Leonhard Euler proved that no walk could cross each of Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once. By treating land and bridges as points and links, he laid the groundwork for graph theory.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: The Starry Night
facts.text: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889 while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The view is based on his window, with an imagined village added. It has been at New York's MoMA since 1941.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Pantheon, Rome
facts.text: The Pantheon in Rome has a concrete dome with a central opening, the oculus. Its interior diameter and height are both about 43 metres, and it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Theremin
facts.text: The theremin is an electronic instrument played without touching it. The player moves their hands near two antennas, one controlling pitch and the other volume. Leon Theremin developed it in 1920.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Pangaea
facts.text: Pangaea was a supercontinent that existed from the late Paleozoic to the early Mesozoic. It came together about 335 million years ago and began to break apart roughly 175 million years ago.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Krakatoa
facts.text: The August 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was among the most violent in recorded history. Its explosions were heard more than 3,000 km away in Perth, and the tsunamis it caused devastated nearby coasts.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Aerogel
facts.text: Aerogels are solid materials that are often 90 to 99.8 percent air by volume. Their tiny, airy structure blocks heat flow, making them extremely good thermal insulators.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Voynich manuscript
facts.text: The Voynich manuscript is a medieval book written in an unknown script that no one has convincingly deciphered. Radiocarbon dating places its vellum in the early 15th century, and it is kept at Yale.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Haiku
facts.text: Haiku is a short Japanese poetic form. Traditionally it uses 17 sound units in three parts of 5, 7 and 5, and often includes a seasonal word and a 'cutting word' that creates a pause.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Panama Canal
facts.text: The Panama Canal opened in 1914 and links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Locks lift ships up to the artificial Gatun Lake, about 26 metres above sea level, and lower them again on the other side.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Aurora
facts.text: Auroras happen when charged particles from the Sun, carried by the solar wind, interact with Earth's magnetic field and strike gases in the upper atmosphere, making them glow. They appear mostly in rings around the poles.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Svalbard Global Seed Vault
facts.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in 2008 as a backup store for the world's crop seeds. It sits deep inside a mountain on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, where permafrost helps keep it cold.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Origami
facts.text: Origami is the art of folding paper, usually a flat square sheet, into a finished shape. It is traditionally associated with Japan, and modern folders generally avoid cutting or gluing; designs that use cuts are called kirigami.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Don Quijote de la Mancha
facts.text: Don Quijote de la Mancha es una novela escrita por Miguel de Cervantes. La primera parte se publicó en 1605 y la segunda en 1615.
facts.translation: Don Quixote is a novel written by Miguel de Cervantes. The first part was published in 1605 and the second in 1615.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Machu Picchu
facts.text: Machu Picchu es una ciudad inca construida en el siglo XV en los Andes de Perú, a unos 2400 metros sobre el nivel del mar.
facts.translation: Machu Picchu is an Inca city built in the 15th century in the Andes of Peru, about 2,400 meters above sea level.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Río Amazonas
facts.text: El Amazonas tiene más de 7000 kilómetros de largo y lleva tanta agua que aporta cerca de una quinta parte del agua dulce que llega a los océanos. Desemboca en el océano Atlántico, en Brasil.
facts.translation: The Amazon is more than 7,000 kilometers long and carries so much water that it supplies about a fifth of the fresh water reaching the oceans. It flows into the Atlantic Ocean, in Brazil.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Alhambra
facts.text: La Alhambra es un conjunto de palacios, jardines y fortalezas en Granada, España. Fue construida por los reyes nazaríes, y su primer rey, Mohamed I, la comenzó en el siglo XIII.
facts.translation: The Alhambra is a complex of palaces, gardens and fortresses in Granada, Spain. It was built by the Nasrid kings, and the first king, Muhammad I, began it in the 13th century.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Frida Kahlo
facts.text: Frida Kahlo fue una pintora mexicana famosa por sus autorretratos. Nació en 1907 en Coyoacán, en la Casa Azul, que hoy es un museo.
facts.translation: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter famous for her self-portraits. She was born in 1907 in Coyoacán, in the Blue House, which is now a museum.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Chichén Itzá
facts.text: Chichén Itzá es una antigua ciudad maya de la península de Yucatán, en México. Su pirámide más famosa, llamada El Castillo o de Kukulcán, fue elegida una de las nuevas siete maravillas del mundo en 2007.
facts.translation: Chichén Itzá is an ancient Maya city on the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico. Its most famous pyramid, called El Castillo or Kukulcán, was chosen as one of the new seven wonders of the world in 2007.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Salar de Uyuni
facts.text: El salar de Uyuni, en Bolivia, es el desierto de sal más grande del mundo. Está a unos 3650 metros de altura y tiene grandes reservas de litio.
facts.translation: The Uyuni salt flat, in Bolivia, is the largest salt desert in the world. It is about 3,650 meters high and has large lithium reserves.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Paella
facts.text: La paella es un plato de arroz que nació en la región de Valencia, España. El nombre viene de la sartén ancha en la que se cocina.
facts.translation: Paella is a rice dish that originated in the Valencia region of Spain. The name comes from the wide pan in which it is cooked.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Camino de Santiago
facts.text: El Camino de Santiago es un conjunto de rutas de peregrinación que llevan a la tumba del apóstol Santiago, en la catedral de Santiago de Compostela, en Galicia.
facts.translation: The Camino de Santiago is a set of pilgrimage routes leading to the tomb of the apostle James, in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in Galicia.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
facts.text: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is named for a Japanese octopus trap, because the ballooned left ventricular apex with a narrow base resembles the jar. Hikaru Sato described it in 1990. It usually follows a physical or emotional stressor, mostly affects postmenopausal women, and the dysfunction is typically transient.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Bezold–Jarisch reflex
facts.text: The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is a vagally mediated triad of bradycardia, hypotension and hypopnea. Von Bezold and Hirt first saw it in 1867 after injecting Veratrum alkaloids, making it the first recognized chemical reflex. Severe hypovolemia or myocardial ischemia can also trigger it.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Brugada syndrome
facts.text: Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmia disorder with coved ST elevation in leads V1 to V3, yet only about 20% of cases involve SCN5A. Dangerous rhythms often occur at rest or during sleep, and in Thailand and Laos it is a leading cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy young men.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Eisenmenger syndrome
facts.text: In Eisenmenger syndrome, a long-standing left-to-right shunt such as a ventricular septal defect drives pulmonary hypertension until the shunt reverses to right-to-left and causes cyanosis. Victor Eisenmenger described it in 1897, and Paul Wood later gave it his name.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Kounis syndrome
facts.text: Kounis syndrome is acute coronary syndrome triggered by an allergic or hypersensitivity reaction. Mast cell mediators such as histamine and proteases can provoke coronary spasm or plaque rupture. Nicholas Kounis gave the first full description, in 1991.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Torsades de pointes
facts.text: Torsades de pointes is French for 'twisting of the points,' describing how the QRS complexes seem to twist around the baseline. François Dessertenne coined the term in 1966 after seeing it in an 80-year-old woman with intermittent complete AV block. It is classically linked to a prolonged QT interval.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Ventricular assist device
facts.text: Patients with continuous-flow left ventricular assist devices can have a greatly reduced or even absent pulse, because the rotary pump moves blood steadily rather than in beats. Liotta and Crawford implanted the first LVAD in 1963; Liotta and DeBakey achieved the first successful implantation in 1966.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Artificial heart valve
facts.text: The Starr-Edwards caged-ball valve, with a silicone ball inside a cage, was first implanted by Albert Starr in 1960. It remained in use for 47 years until it was retired in 2007, and one valve is reported to have lasted 48 years.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Bainbridge reflex
facts.text: The Bainbridge reflex raises heart rate when the right atrium is stretched by increased venous return. In 1915 Francis Bainbridge infused blood or saline into anesthetized dogs and saw tachycardia that vanished when the vagus was cut. The response depends on the baseline heart rate.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Bioactive glass
facts.text: Bioactive glass, developed by Larry Hench's group at the University of Florida starting in 1969, bonds to bone because its surface converts into a calcium phosphate layer that matures into hydroxyapatite, onto which bone grows. The best-known composition is 45S5, trademarked as Bioglass.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Alpha-gal syndrome
facts.text: Alpha-gal syndrome is an IgE-mediated allergy to the carbohydrate galactose-α-1,3-galactose found in mammalian meat. Unlike most food allergies, reactions typically begin 2 to 8 hours after eating. It is acquired after tick bites, and was uncovered when reactions to cetuximab led Thomas Platts-Mills's team to the same antibody.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Original antigenic sin
facts.text: Original antigenic sin is the tendency of the immune system to reuse memory from a first infection when it meets a drifted variant of a pathogen, which can blunt a fresh response. Thomas Francis Jr. coined it in 1960 from influenza work, as a play on the theological idea of original sin.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Microchimerism
facts.text: Microchimerism means carrying a small number of cells from another individual. After pregnancy, fetal cells can persist in the mother for decades; one study found male fetal cells in maternal blood 27 years later. Their health effects, including in autoimmune disease, remain unclear.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Biofilm
facts.text: Biofilms are microbial communities embedded in a self-made matrix of polysaccharides, proteins and DNA. Cells inside can tolerate antibiotics at levels far above those that kill free-floating cells, and biofilms often form on implanted devices such as catheters and prosthetic heart valves.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Refeeding syndrome
facts.text: Refeeding syndrome is a metabolic disturbance that follows restoring nutrition in a starved person. Returning insulin drives cells to take up phosphate, potassium and magnesium that are already depleted, so serum phosphate falls and ATP stores drop. It was probably first identified during the 1944–45 Dutch famine.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Theralizumab
facts.text: In March 2006, six healthy volunteers at a London phase 1 trial received TGN1412, a CD28 superagonist antibody, at about 1/500 of the highest dose given to macaques. All six were hospitalized within about 16 hours with severe cytokine release. Macaque effector memory T cells lack CD28, which explains why animal tests missed the risk.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Nickel titanium
facts.text: Nitinol's name combines nickel, titanium and the Naval Ordnance Laboratory, where William Buehler's team was seeking fatigue-resistant alloys for missile nose cones. Its shape memory and superelasticity let a collapsed stent spring back to its expanded shape once warmed to body temperature.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Immune privilege
facts.text: Immune privilege shields tissues such as the eye, testis and fetus from damaging immune responses. Mechanisms include limited lymphatic drainage, low MHC expression and constitutive Fas ligand, which restricts entry of Fas-expressing lymphocytes. In the eye, anterior chamber–associated immune deviation actively suppresses systemic responses.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 长城
facts.text: 长城很长，是中国古代的人建的，为了保护国家。
facts.translation: The Great Wall is very long. People in ancient China built it to protect the country.
facts.reading: Chángchéng hěn cháng, shì Zhōngguó gǔdài de rén jiàn de, wèile bǎohù guójiā.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 大熊猫
facts.text: 大熊猫几乎只吃竹子，大部分住在中国的四川。
facts.translation: Giant pandas eat almost only bamboo, and most of them live in Sichuan, China.
facts.reading: Dà xióngmāo jīhū zhǐ chī zhúzi, dà bùfen zhù zài Zhōngguó de Sìchuān.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 故宫
facts.text: 故宫在北京，是明朝和清朝皇帝住的地方，1420年建好。
facts.translation: The Forbidden City is in Beijing. It is where the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties lived, and it was finished in 1420.
facts.reading: Gùgōng zài Běijīng, shì Míngcháo hé Qīngcháo huángdì zhù de dìfang, 1420 nián jiàn hǎo.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 春节
facts.text: 春节是农历新年，除夕晚上，一家人在一起吃团圆饭。
facts.translation: The Spring Festival is the lunar new year. On New Year's Eve, the whole family eats a reunion dinner together.
facts.reading: Chūnjié shì nónglì xīnnián, chúxī wǎnshang, yījiārén zài yìqǐ chī tuányuánfàn.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 黄河
facts.text: 黄河是中国第二长的河，河水里有很多泥沙，所以是黄色的。
facts.translation: The Yellow River is the second longest river in China. Its water has a lot of silt, so it is yellow.
facts.reading: Huánghé shì Zhōngguó dì-èr cháng de hé, héshuǐ lǐ yǒu hěn duō níshā, suǒyǐ shì huángsè de.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 造纸术
facts.text: 造纸术是中国的四大发明之一，人们说汉代的蔡伦让造纸更好了。
facts.translation: Papermaking is one of China's Four Great Inventions. People say Cai Lun of the Han dynasty made papermaking better.
facts.reading: Zàozhǐshù shì Zhōngguó de sì dà fāmíng zhī yī, rénmen shuō Hàndài de Cài Lún ràng zàozhǐ gèng hǎo le.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 珠穆朗玛峰
facts.text: 珠穆朗玛峰是世界上最高的山，在中国和尼泊尔中间，高八千八百多米。
facts.translation: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. It is between China and Nepal and is over 8,800 meters high.
facts.reading: Zhūmùlǎngmǎ Fēng shì shìjiè shàng zuì gāo de shān, zài Zhōngguó hé Níbó'ěr zhōngjiān, gāo bāqiān bābǎi duō mǐ.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 中秋节
facts.text: 中秋节在农历八月十五，这一天人们常常吃月饼。
facts.translation: The Mid-Autumn Festival is on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, and people often eat mooncakes on this day.
facts.reading: Zhōngqiūjié zài nónglì bāyuè shíwǔ, zhè yì tiān rénmen chángcháng chī yuèbǐng.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 茶
facts.text: 茶是用茶树的叶子做的饮料，最早出现在中国。
facts.translation: Tea is a drink made from tea plant leaves, and it first appeared in China.
facts.reading: Chá shì yòng cháshù de yèzi zuò de yǐnliào, zuì zǎo chūxiàn zài Zhōngguó.
